rows.caveat: Apple ecosystem fit and storage needs are unknown. Key custom-domain article was published after the question date; historical equivalence is not established.

rows.name: Infomaniak Mail Service
rows.application_scope: Standalone domain email service with the Android Mail app; household account permissions require confirmation.
rows.reason: Potentially inexpensive multi-address domain hosting with a documented first-party Android application.
rows.caveat: Final family quote, independent family-user access and the chosen platform configuration are unverified. The public repository identifies an Android app but implementation-level native behavior and polish were not audited.

rows.name: mailbox Standard with a separately selected native client
rows.application_scope: Email hosting plus a native mail client selected and configured separately using the documented mail protocols.
rows.reason: Custom-domain and family hosting at a modest per-person price, if an independent native client is acceptable.
rows.caveat: No provider-owned native email app was verified. Family accounts are separately billed. Confirm one thing: may the native client be separate from the provider? If yes, validate the chosen client's configuration; if no, this candidate remains insufficient unless a first-party app is documented.

rows.name: HEY
rows.application_scope: HEY personal or family email through its own apps; choose separately priced Domains service if a custom domain is wanted.
rows.reason: Explicit native-app documentation and a family offer, with materially higher costs when a custom domain is desired.
rows.caveat: Family pricing uses hey.com addresses. Domain hosting has a different per-user price, and off-the-shelf third-party clients are unsupported. The user's subjective polish preference still needs a trial.

rows.name: iCloud+ Mail with Apple Mail
rows.application_scope: Hosted family email integrated with Apple devices.
rows.reason: iCloud+ supplies inexpensive custom-domain email and family sharing through Apple's native Mail application for an Apple-centered household.
rows.caveat: Observed US starting price is USD 0.99/month; shared storage also serves other iCloud uses, and the native app fit depends on Apple platforms.

rows.name: Fastmail
rows.application_scope: Complete hosted personal/family email service.
rows.reason: Fastmail combines its own installed email apps, custom-domain hosting and a six-person Family subscription in the closest overall fit to the requested package.
rows.caveat: USD 132/year Family or USD 60/year Individual at observed US pricing; app-download availability does not prove a fully native UI, subjective polish, or availability by the cutoff.

rows.name: mailbox.org with Thunderbird or Apple Mail
rows.application_scope: Alternative mechanism separating the hosting provider from the native application.
rows.reason: mailbox.org can provide the custom-domain and family-account backend while a separately chosen native client supplies the preferred email interface.
rows.caveat: It is a two-component setup, not a verified first-party native app package; each family account is charged separately and calendar/contact integration needs care.

rows.name: Fastmail
rows.application_scope: Personal email hosting using a listed Fastmail installed application; no particular native UI toolkit is assumed.
rows.reason: Best documented combination of installed apps, custom-domain hosting and flat family pricing.
rows.caveat: Polish was not tested. App internals and historical availability on the question date remain unknown. Confirm that installed applications satisfy the intended meaning of native.

rows.name: Infomaniak Mail with Mail Service or kSuite
rows.application_scope: Custom-domain email hosting with first-party iOS and Android apps.
rows.reason: Infomaniak offers its own mobile mail applications alongside economical custom-domain hosting that can cover several household mailboxes.
rows.caveat: The generic-domain personal offering differs from custom-domain Mail Service/kSuite; calculate actual mailbox charges and trial the interface rather than assuming a flat family bundle or a desktop app.

rows.name: Zoho Mail
rows.application_scope: Hosted domain email for separate household users, using Zoho clients.
rows.reason: Zoho Mail provides custom-domain accounts and mobile/desktop application options at low per-user entry pricing when a business-style administration model is acceptable.
rows.caveat: No flat family plan verified; Desktop Lite is a web-style installed client, while Trident's native desktop option and plan entitlement should be confirmed; indexed pricing is not a final regional quote.

rows.name: Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507, Q6_K or Q8_0 GGUF
rows.application_scope: Lower-memory, direct-response extraction baseline.
rows.reason: Its dedicated non-thinking instruction behavior and 3.31 GB Q6_K or 4.28 GB Q8_0 files make it a practical compact baseline for direct structured retain extraction.
rows.caveat: No matched gpt-oss-20b retain evaluation was located; nominal 256K model context cannot be assumed to fit 8 GB, and longer inputs still need bounded processing.

rows.name: llama.cpp schema-constrained generation and explicit GPU placement
rows.application_scope: Supporting mechanism shared by the candidate models, not a model replacement.
rows.reason: Schema-constrained JSON plus explicit GPU-layer and context controls can make a smaller local extractor operationally usable and expose whether it meets the no-spill requirement.
rows.caveat: Schema validity does not guarantee correct facts; architecture/build support and maximum-workload VRAM must be checked, and CPU orchestration is distinct from model-weight spill.

rows.name: Qwen3.5-9B, Q4_K_M GGUF
rows.application_scope: Quality-focused alternative to the 4B extractor.
rows.reason: The 9B member supplies a stronger published instruction-following option with a 5.68 GB Q4_K_M file that could fit the 8 GB GPU at controlled context and concurrency.
rows.caveat: The smaller remaining memory margin makes this conditional on actual Windows VRAM, cache and compute-buffer use; no retain parity or no-spill fit is proven.

rows.name: Qwen3.5-4B, preferably Q6_K GGUF
rows.application_scope: Primary local retain extraction model; text-only inference through llama.cpp.
rows.reason: A 4B model with strong published instruction-following results and a 3.53 GB Q6_K GGUF offers a promising retain extractor while preserving substantial room for GPU context and runtime buffers.
rows.caveat: Published benchmarks are not Hindsight retain results and do not establish quantized parity with gpt-oss-20b; require compatible llama.cpp, explicit context limits and a measured full-GPU allocation.

rows.name: Ministral 3 8B Instruct 2512, Q4_K_M GGUF
rows.application_scope: Independent dense-model family for structured extraction comparison.
rows.reason: This dense alternative offers native JSON/function-calling behavior and a 5.2 GB Q4_K_M GGUF that could support a local retain pipeline within a carefully measured 8 GB configuration.
rows.caveat: The official FP8 configuration targets 12 GB; the 8 GB route needs further quantization and bounded context, and neither retain quality nor Windows full-GPU fit was tested.

rows.name: JArgs
rows.application_scope: The option-parsing layer of a parseOptions(String) adapter after quote-aware tokenization.
rows.reason: JArgs supplies a compact BSD-licensed GNU-style Java option parser with grouped boolean short flags, long options and -- termination.
rows.caveat: Takes String[] and exposes accessors rather than returning Map; clusters cannot contain value-taking options according to its exception documentation; the single-file ideal was not verified.

rows.name: JArgs (option-recognition component)
rows.application_scope: Narrowly parsing already-tokenized arguments and retrieving options/operands through accessors.
rows.reason: A compact BSD-licensed parser with documented GNU-like flags is a plausible small backend, provided the string-input and returned-result wrapper is supplied.
caveat: parse(String[]) returns void and is followed by accessors; it does not itself supply the requested whole-string/result function.
The proposed adapter must tokenize quotes, call parse(String[]), and gather options and remaining operands; no integration was executed.
Short boolean flags can be grouped, but value-taking flags have grouping restrictions.
Single-file distribution and complete platform support were not verified.

rows.name: Apache Commons CLI DefaultParser
rows.application_scope: Parse tokenized arguments into CommandLine, then adapt the result to application-owned Map and operand structures.
rows.reason: Commons CLI provides short-option bursting and configurable option parsing that can supply the Java shell's option-recognition layer.
rows.caveat: Requires String[] and its own result classes; not one file; current source corroboration of long-option and terminator behavior is not automatically historical evidence.

rows.name: Apache Ant Commandline.translateCommandline
rows.application_scope: Raw-string tokenization front end, complementary to candidates 1–3.
rows.reason: Ant's String-to-String[] tokenizer can preserve quoted spaces before one of the Java option parsers processes options.
rows.caveat: Not an option parser; its limited quote-and-space grammar is not a complete shell lexer; unbalanced quotes are errors; live evidence was not dated before cutoff.

rows.name: JOpt Simple (option-recognition component)
rows.application_scope: Narrowly the token-array option-recognition stage; not offered as a standalone whole-string parser.
rows.reason: Documents the required option conventions clearly and offers MIT licensing, but a separate string-tokenization and result adapter is needed.
caveat: parse(String...) consumes argument tokens rather than lexing a complete command string.
Proposed mapping is CommandLineTokenizer.tokenize(String) -> String[] -> OptionParser.parse -> OptionSet -> optional user-facing Map wrapper; not implemented or run.
Tokenizer errors would lose quoted whitespace before option recognition.
The opened 6.0-alpha-3 documentation postdates the question; historical release behavior is unverified.
Complete platform/runtime support and exact GNU equivalence beyond listed conventions remain unverified.

rows.name: JOpt Simple
rows.application_scope: Array-based option parser with standard Map export.
rows.reason: JOpt Simple combines getopt-style clusters, long options and -- handling with an OptionSet.asMap() result useful for an application adapter.
rows.caveat: Requires a tokenizer for raw strings; map keys are OptionSpec objects; inspected documentation is from 2018 and older exact behavior was not dated in this run.

rows.name: JSAP
rows.application_scope: Whole option-parser component within the existing Java shell; evaluate manual v2.1 behavior.
rows.reason: The documented parse(String) API directly matches the requested input shape and supports quoted spaces, with several mandatory option behaviors still unverified.
caveat: Clustered flags, exact long equals handling, -- termination and full cross-platform support remain unverified.
Tokenizer is documented as Windows-style, so full Unix-shell semantics cannot be assumed.
Manual v2.1 says LGPL; non-copyleft is only a preference.
Returns JSAPResult rather than a built-in Map; no single-file claim verified.

rows.name: Veusz
rows.application_scope: Dedicated scientific figure production from tabular data.
rows.reason: Veusz offers a graphical workflow for turning experimental data into publication-ready figures with error bars, labels, multiple panels and vector export.
rows.caveat: Its widget-based layout takes some learning; current 3D features were not established for the 2016 cutoff.

rows.name: SciDAVis
rows.application_scope: Complete stand-alone application for scientific data plotting.
rows.reason: Closest documented conceptual match to the user's Origin/SigmaPlot-style graphical scientific plotting workflow.
rows.caveat: Community routes exist, but relative adoption and responsiveness were not established. The GUI mission statement is dated after the question; precise 2016 behavior remains unverified. Extra analysis features are allowed by the request.

rows.name: LabPlot
rows.application_scope: Scientific desktop plotting and reusable projects based on imported or spreadsheet data.
rows.reason: LabPlot provides interactive plot creation, layout and curve editing using spreadsheet data, allowing the requested GUI plotting workflow without requiring statistical analysis.
rows.caveat: The 2016 release described Windows support as new and less mature than Linux; later platform and analysis features should not be projected backward.

rows.name: Grace
rows.application_scope: Complete application for 2D data plots; no requirement for 3D or terrain-specific functions was stated.
rows.reason: Direct point-and-click alternative for two-dimensional scientific plotting, especially in a Unix/X11 environment.
rows.caveat: The official platform description centers on Unix/X11 and mentions older Windows ports; compatibility with an unspecified modern OS is unverified. A linked forum does not establish audience size or response quality.

rows.name: Gnumeric
rows.application_scope: Quick charts from modest tabular datasets using a familiar spreadsheet workflow.
rows.reason: Gnumeric can turn selected spreadsheet cells into charts through a graphical wizard and supports visual editing and export for straightforward plotting tasks.
rows.caveat: A spreadsheet is a narrower fit for specialized scientific figures or surface visualization; the opened chart guide is undated.

rows.name: Veusz
rows.application_scope: Complete stand-alone plotting application; the GUI is the proposed interface.
rows.reason: Focused GUI plotting application with composable graph elements and documented scientific plot/export features.
rows.caveat: Widget-based editing may require learning. Current support links do not prove popularity. The opened README is version 4.2.1, so its present-day features must not be assumed available in 2016; optional scripting is not a conflict.

rows.name: Kst
rows.application_scope: Exploratory viewing of large measurement datasets and changing data streams.
rows.reason: Kst provides graphical plotting and mouse-driven exploration of large or streaming scientific datasets, with matrix displays and image or vector export.
rows.caveat: Its emphasis on data exploration may be less natural for highly composed static figures, and the opened live documentation has no established historical date.

rows.name: SciDAVis
rows.application_scope: Interactive scientific plotting in a desktop table and matrix workspace.
rows.reason: SciDAVis supplies a table-and-plot graphical workspace with 2D, 3D and multilayer plotting that suits scientists moving from commercial plotting packages.
rows.caveat: The opened handbook is later than the cutoff, so detailed historical feature parity is unverified; the official repository identifies scidavis.org as unaffiliated.

rows.name: Grace
rows.application_scope: Detailed 2D scientific plotting, especially on Unix-like desktop systems.
rows.reason: Grace offers precise point-and-click editing of 2D scientific graphs and vector export for users who mainly need conventional curves and annotations.
rows.caveat: Its X/Motif interface and platform requirements are less convenient for some desktop users, and it is not a complete 3D surface-plotting replacement.

rows.name: LabPlot
rows.application_scope: Complete application for importing data, creating plots and exporting figures.
rows.reason: Graphical scientific plotting with spreadsheet/imported-data workflows and documented community support routes.
rows.caveat: Current features/platforms and support routes are later evidence. The July 2016 source describes Windows delivery as upcoming and a Mac port as a hope; it does not verify successful 2016 installation. User counts and first-hand ease were not assessed.

rows.name: Symfony with Symfony UX
rows.application_scope: Alternative application framework and UI integration ecosystem for rebuilding the site around retained domain behavior.
rows.reason: A PHP alternative with documented Stimulus integration and UX components offers an explicit route to charts and interactive server-rendered pages.
rows.caveat: The opened UX overview does not prove compatibility with the unseen legacy code or completion of all workflows. Custom drag/drop persistence and spreadsheet/payment integration remain necessary. Present-day notices about Symfony 6.2 maintenance must not be interpreted as its January 2023 status.

rows.name: Chart.js
rows.application_scope: Statistical chart presentation.
rows.reason: Chart.js can render graphs of backend-computed component usage counts.
rows.caveat: Does not calculate business usage metrics; inspected evidence is later than the question cutoff, and version 3.9.1 retrieval failed.

rows.name: Laravel Cashier for Stripe
rows.application_scope: Payment-provider integration.
rows.reason: Cashier's payment and subscription integration could support prepaid service purchases and account billing if Stripe matches the payment arrangement.
rows.caveat: Prepaid credits and entitlement accounting still require application logic; subscription billing is not automatically the right prepaid model.

rows.name: Vue 3 over the existing PHP/Perl backend
rows.application_scope: Frontend framework only; existing account, domain, database, export and prepaid services remain behind HTML or authenticated endpoints.
rows.reason: Incremental frontend replacement minimizes the initial backend migration surface and offers a documented path from existing server-rendered pages to richer interaction.
rows.caveat: Vue is a partial solution. Endpoint design, authorization, drag/drop synchronization, list rendering performance and the availability of reusable backend operations remain application work.

rows.name: Livewire 2
rows.application_scope: Server-driven interactive application UI.
rows.reason: Livewire's PHP-and-Blade components can implement interactive selection, forms, and group-management screens without full page reloads.
rows.caveat: Keep drag motion client-side and prototype complex editor state; versioned live documentation has no verified publication date.

rows.name: Inertia.js with Vue and Laravel
rows.application_scope: Alternative frontend architecture for a stateful drag-and-drop editor.
rows.reason: Inertia connects a Vue component-based editor to Laravel routing and controllers for richer browser-side interaction.
rows.caveat: Requires learning modern JavaScript components and a build workflow; Inertia's own opened page had no readable body, so verification relies on Laravel's primary documentation.

rows.name: Laravel 9 with Breeze
rows.application_scope: Primary PHP application framework and authentication scaffolding.
rows.reason: Laravel provides a PHP application foundation and Breeze scaffolds authentication for the site's account and database workflows.
rows.caveat: Requires modern PHP and explicit adaptation of legacy PHP/Perl logic; the starter-kit page itself is undated.

rows.name: Laravel Excel 3.1
rows.application_scope: Excel export integration.
rows.reason: Laravel Excel can turn the requesting user's selected components and groups into a downloadable Excel workbook.
rows.caveat: Export queries require user scoping, explicit columns, and memory assessment for large datasets.

rows.name: Laravel with Livewire and small JavaScript components
rows.application_scope: Primary framework stack for the rebuilt application; retain or wrap domain logic, then build account, persistence and presentation workflows around it.
rows.reason: A PHP-centered rebuild with documented reactive components is a plausible starting point for the existing PHP site, while dedicated JavaScript can handle drag-and-drop.
rows.caveat: Legacy PHP compatibility, the Perl boundary and delivery effort are unverified. Laravel 9 requires PHP 8.0 or newer; this is a documented dependency, not a contradiction because the user's runtime is unspecified. Livewire does not by itself establish the required grouping interface, thousand-item performance, prepaid flow or Excel behavior.

rows.name: Laravel with Inertia.js and Vue
rows.application_scope: Alternative full application stack to the Livewire route, using Laravel on the server and Vue for the browser interface.
rows.reason: A documented bridge combines Laravel controllers with Vue pages when the grouping workspace needs substantial client-side state.
rows.caveat: Requires learning a Vue/component workflow and asset tooling as well as handling the legacy PHP/Perl boundary. No comparative delivery-time or thousand-item interaction benchmark was obtained.

rows.name: SortableJS
rows.application_scope: Browser drag-and-drop interaction.
rows.reason: SortableJS provides cross-list dragging, grouping, and stable-ID serialization for moving components between saved groups.
rows.caveat: Persistence, account authorization, business rules, and large-list rendering remain application responsibilities.

rows.name: Django 4.1
rows.application_scope: Alternative Python application framework.
rows.reason: Django offers database models, routing, and an administrative interface as an alternative foundation for component and group management.
rows.caveat: Changing language requires translating or exposing old PHP/Perl logic, and the custom customer editor still must be built.

rows.name: Cyclos 3.6
rows.application_scope: Community payments, account management, loan and fee workflows, with third-party integration.
rows.reason: Cyclos 3.6 can provide member accounts, balances, payment authorizations, scheduled payments and loans for a community-oriented financial service.
rows.caveat: A general ledger and any required external banking connections need checking; the current official Cyclos 3 page says it is unmaintained and discourages mission-critical use, so it is a historical candidate rather than an unqualified current deployment recommendation.

rows.name: GnuCash
rows.application_scope: Accounting-only component: ledger entries, account registers and financial records.
rows.reason: GnuCash can cover the double-entry ledger and accounting portion if the credit union chooses a separate member-account and payment system.
rows.caveat: The evidence supports personal and small-business accounting, not an all-in-one credit-union core or a multiuser teller/payment-processing deployment.

rows.name: Mifos X
rows.application_scope: Primary core-banking shortlist: savings, loans, payment-related transfers and financial accounting.
rows.reason: Mifos X can supply the credit union's core member savings and lending operations, account transfers and integrated accounting through a configurable open-source banking platform.
rows.caveat: External payment-network connectivity and local reporting requirements still need evaluation; this research did not test a 400–1,000-member installation.

rows.name: OpenCBS Desktop
rows.application_scope: Whole candidate for client, loan, savings, payment-recording and accounting operations; evaluate Desktop/free core specifically, not the later Cloud service.
rows.reason: A plausible core-banking alternative with an open-source desktop edition, loan and savings operations, repayment recording and configurable accounting rules; the ledger boundary of the free core needs confirmation.
rows.caveat: The official repository describes Desktop development during 2013-2017. The 14.11 manual's exact date was not established. It distinguishes free-core functionality from paid modules and a configured accounting engine, so the Cloud feature matrix is not evidence for the Desktop edition. No throughput test or external clearing integration was verified.

rows.name: Cyclos 3
rows.application_scope: Whole candidate under investigation for member banking and payment operations; no claim that account histories alone satisfy the complete ledger requirement.
rows.reason: A version-specific open-source option with member accounts, payment functions and loans, but the institutional ledger requirement is unresolved and the developer now advises against mission-critical deployment.
rows.caveat: This is Cyclos 3 only. The official live page says it is no longer maintained and advises against mission-critical use. Maintenance was not an explicit user requirement, so this is a material caveat rather than an invented exclusion. Full institutional ledger coverage and exact release suitability for 400-1,000 members were not established.

rows.name: OpenCBS Desktop
rows.application_scope: Microfinance core and repayment operations, with plugin-based connections to accounting, POS and web services.
rows.reason: OpenCBS Desktop could manage clients, loans, repayments and savings while integrating a separate accounting or payment component.
rows.caveat: The opened material does not establish availability before 2014-09-15; available release files are from 2016–2017, and the live project page says Desktop is unsupported after replacement by Cloud in 2019.

rows.name: S.A.F.E. Open Source Microfinance Suite
rows.application_scope: Integrated microfinance suite; present-day project listing includes loan, cashier, accounting, savings and bank modules.
rows.reason: SAFE offers a microfinance-oriented starting point for combining lending, cash handling, savings and accounting in a small financial institution.
rows.caveat: The June 2014 release notes warn of difficult configuration and partial English translation; the live module list is later evidence and does not establish that every named module existed in the 2014 release.

rows.name: Mifos X
rows.application_scope: Whole candidate for the credit union's operational core, using Mifos X's own open-source platform and interface; no proprietary mLite front end is assumed.
rows.reason: The strongest starting point for an open-source core: dated project material documents lending, integrated accounting and savings, with the exact payment workflow and 2014 configuration still to verify.
rows.caveat: The 2013 initial release was individual-lending oriented. A July 2013 article documents savings and MPL 2.0 but has a December 2014 modification timestamp. Payment integrations cannot be inferred from a proprietary M-Pesa application. The 1.25 repayment/accrual announcement is after the question. Exact 400-1,000-member deployment sizing and institution-specific workflows were not tested.

rows.name: OGDF (Open Graph Drawing Framework)
rows.application_scope: whole C++ graph-library alternative; graph/data-structure layer can be used without making visualization the task
rows.reason: A documented C++ graph library with broad structural mutation and associated attributes; its adjacency-list representation and GPL terms introduce concrete tradeoffs to evaluate.
rows.caveat: The opened API is 2023.09, after the question date. Full Boost dependency closure and requested performance are unverified. Edge lookup is degree-dependent. GPL v2/v3 with exceptions may fit the license preference less well.

rows.name: SNAP (Stanford Network Analysis Platform)
rows.application_scope: whole C++ graph-library alternative; choose directed/undirected graph and richer network containers according to semantics
rows.reason: Best documented broad fit found: self-contained C++ graph/network containers with dynamic structure, rich node/edge data, and explicit large-network design.
rows.caveat: Uses its own GLib-style types. Modern C++11 idioms, filtered-query performance, exact move semantics and strongly skewed-degree performance were not established. Benchmark the concrete workload.

rows.name: LEMON
rows.application_scope: whole C++ graph-library alternative; investigate mutable ListGraph/ListDigraph rather than assuming every representation supports all edits
rows.reason: A promising C++ graph-library alternative with permissive source licensing and indexed evidence of mutable ListGraph/ListDigraph APIs, but several required properties could not be fully verified.
rows.caveat: Official tutorial and graph documentation opens were blocked; attempted source-file opens also failed. Significant-Boost-dependency absence, degree behavior, performance, and exact semantics remain unverified. Boost Software License is a license name, not evidence of Boost code use.

rows.name: NetworKit C++ core
rows.application_scope: Sparse-network analysis, graph iteration, directed/undirected conversion, and parallel algorithms.
rows.reason: NetworKit provides a native C++ graph-analysis core with historical support for directed graphs and indexed edge attributes, making it a useful candidate when scalable traversal and analytics dominate.
rows.caveat: The project emphasizes analytics and Python integration; exact historical mutation costs, high-degree deletion behavior, arbitrary payload ergonomics, and absence of significant Boost dependencies were not fully verified. Present-day storage/API additions must not be assumed available in 2016.

rows.name: LLAMA — mutable multiversioned CSR graph storage
rows.application_scope: Storage-mechanism alternative for large graphs, consistent analytical snapshots, and optional out-of-memory operation.
rows.reason: LLAMA is a C++11 storage alternative that combines updates with compact CSR snapshots and node/edge properties for workloads that alternate incoming changes with whole-graph analysis.
rows.caveat: This is a research-oriented storage engine rather than a simple drop-in graph container; the README flags unfinished streaming integration and a broken persistent deletion configuration. A complete directed/undirected convenience API and arbitrary mutation behavior were not verified.

rows.name: SNAP — Stanford Network Analysis Platform
rows.application_scope: Large in-memory networks with traversal, filtering/subgraph extraction, and custom semantics on nodes or edges.
rows.reason: SNAP supplies directed and undirected graphs, mutable network operations, and templated vertex/edge data types for large sparse-network analysis.
rows.caveat: Its custom GLib containers, pointers, and iterator conventions are an integration commitment rather than a modern standard-library-style API; historical releases include breaking changes and deletion fixes. No workload-specific performance or full dependency/license audit was performed.

rows.name: OGDF — Open Graph Drawing Framework
rows.application_scope: General graph algorithms and representation, with particular strength in planarity, decomposition, graph drawing, and associated metadata.
rows.reason: OGDF offers a self-contained C++ graph representation, node/edge associative arrays, and reusable graph algorithms for applications that also benefit from topology manipulation or drawing.
rows.caveat: GPL licensing conflicts with the preference for a permissive license, and a drawing-oriented library may add unnecessary scope. The opened material does not establish favorable allocation behavior or performance for this particular mutation-heavy workload.

rows.name: LEMON — ListDigraph/ListGraph with selectable graph representations
rows.application_scope: General-purpose in-process graph storage and algorithms; List types for mutation, Smart types for append-oriented use, StaticDigraph for fixed directed graphs.
rows.reason: LEMON offers mutable directed and undirected graph types, maps for associated data, and alternative representations that directly address the tradeoff between flexible updates and compact traversal.
rows.caveat: Smart types do not support arbitrary deletion and StaticDigraph is immutable; mutations can invalidate affected iterators and removed IDs may be reused. C++11 style, complete dependency/license verification, and the exact version publication date remain unverified in the opened evidence.

rows.name: Argtable3
rows.application_scope: Whole parser alternative using argument tables.
rows.reason: Declarative ANSI C parser with generated help, multiple aliases and repeated occurrences, pending pass-through verification.
rows.caveat: Unmatched-option recovery is the main unresolved fit issue. Current maintenance, macOS coverage, separate-value long options and repeat override/order details were not established within this discovery budget.

rows.name: GLib GOption
rows.application_scope: Whole command-line parsing library requirement, using GLib's GOption component.
rows.reason: Best documented partial-parsing fit, with declarative entries, generated help and repeated string arrays.
rows.caveat: Larger utility-library dependency. Unknown-option values are inherently ambiguous when mixed with positional arguments. Exact scalar overwrite behavior, array encounter order and explicit macOS evidence remain unverified. Subcommand dispatch would need a separately verified design.

rows.name: argparse (C library)
rows.application_scope: Whole parser alternative; application callbacks may be required for aggregation.
rows.reason: Small high-level C alternative with generated help, aliases, callback hooks and an ignore-unknown flag.
rows.caveat: Three-platform maintenance evidence, exact unknown-token preservation, both value spellings and repeat policies remain unverified. Initializer macros are visible but are a preference issue rather than a mandatory exclusion.

rows.name: GNU Gengetopt
rows.application_scope: Alternative build-time code-generation mechanism rather than a handwritten runtime argument loop.
rows.reason: Gengetopt generates C parsing code from an option specification, reducing duplication while supporting aliases, both long-value forms and repeated-value arrays.
rows.caveat: Unknown-option forwarding and native subcommands remain unverified; getopt_long portability and current maintenance require checking, particularly for native Windows builds.

rows.name: Argtable3
rows.application_scope: Small embeddable parser with a single-file distribution and little option-definition boilerplate.
rows.reason: Argtable3 turns a declarative ANSI C table into parsing and usage output, with positional values, repeated typed arguments and multiple short/long aliases.
rows.caveat: Transparent unknown-option preservation, last-occurrence overriding and native subcommands were not established; current maintenance at the cutoff was not independently dated.

rows.name: cofyc/argparse
rows.application_scope: Compact C implementation and callback-based extension point for an application-specific parser.
rows.reason: This MIT-licensed high-level C parser supplies automatic help and positional/optional arguments, while its public header exposes unknown-argument and stop-at-non-option modes.
rows.caveat: The header flags alone do not prove exact preservation behavior; ordered aggregation, overriding, both long-value forms, three-platform builds, subcommands, macro burden and maintenance need further verification.

rows.name: GLib GOption / GOptionContext
rows.application_scope: Primary parser candidate, particularly when adding the GLib dependency is acceptable.
rows.reason: GOption provides declarative C option entries, generated help, short/long aliases, both long-value forms, positional collection, repeated string arrays and an explicit mode preserving unknown options.
rows.caveat: Unknown options followed by separate values can be ambiguous; use an explicit forwarding convention. Native subcommands and exact repeated-scalar override semantics were not verified. GLib is a larger dependency; dated maintenance evidence at the cutoff was not established.

rows.name: NLog with DatabaseTarget and a local File target
rows.application_scope: Whole requested logging feature within the existing C#/WPF application, using NLog plus its database target and a compatible ADO.NET provider.

rows.name: PostgreSQL job ledger with unique task keys and atomic permanent claims
rows.application_scope: Whole proposed task-distribution configuration, including application-written workers and a durable identity ledger.
rows.reason: The clearest configurable starting point separates durable admission deduplication from exclusive worker claims and makes the no-retry tradeoff explicit.
rows.caveat: Strict at-most-once start requires recording a permanent claim before execution and never automatically re-running an uncertain claim; crashes can strand work. Transactional or idempotent outputs solve a different, weaker duplicate-effects problem. Confirm task identity and acceptable failure recovery before treating this as a complete answer.

rows.name: Celery Once (QueueOnce)
rows.application_scope: Reusable admission-lock component for a Celery deployment.
rows.reason: QueueOnce adds a task-identity lock around Celery submission so equivalent pending or running tasks can be rejected before another copy is queued.
rows.caveat: The default one-hour lock can expire during queued-plus-running time; direct calls and retry behavior need review, and the lock is not permanent completion deduplication.

rows.name: Bull job IDs and renewable job locks
rows.application_scope: Node.js and Redis queue with job identity, retries, and worker ownership.
rows.reason: Bull combines existing-jobId rejection with renewable Redis job locks to reduce duplicate queue entries and concurrent handling in Node.js workers.
rows.caveat: Stalled recovery can repeat processing; job deletion removes the retained identity, and CPU-bound handlers can interfere with lock renewal.

rows.name: pg-boss
rows.application_scope: Potential whole library alternative for a Node.js application, conditional on matching its policies to both duplicate prohibitions.
rows.reason: A Node.js/PostgreSQL queue packages the same claim mechanism and transaction integration, but its deduplication, retry and expiry policies need release-specific verification.
rows.caveat: The search snippet claimed exactly-once delivery, but the actually opened README instead describes concurrent claims and atomic commits. Automatic retries are listed. Those facts do not prove task bodies never execute twice; no exact deduplication/timeout configuration was verified.

rows.name: PostgreSQL unique job ledger with ON CONFLICT and FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
rows.application_scope: Language-independent durable admission registry, claim ownership, and transactional result recording.
rows.reason: A unique logical job key can reject duplicate registration while transactional SKIP LOCKED claims assign different pending jobs to concurrent workers.
rows.caveat: Short claim transactions need explicit leases and recovery; external effects still require idempotency or a shared transaction, and stale workers must not commit after losing ownership.

rows.name: pg-boss
rows.application_scope: PostgreSQL-backed Node.js job execution for an existing relational stack.
rows.reason: pg-boss packages PostgreSQL SKIP LOCKED job claiming behind Node.js send-and-work APIs, reducing the amount of custom queue plumbing.
rows.caveat: The opened page confirms claims, not a complete guarantee against duplicate logical registration or arbitrary external effects; current deduplication and long-job options require further verification.

rows.name: Celery 4.2 with a RabbitMQ broker
rows.application_scope: Python task execution with independently scalable worker pools for long and short jobs.
rows.reason: Celery supplies distributed task workers, routing and acknowledgment controls for executing the workload once durable job admission and idempotent effects are supplied.
rows.caveat: Celery alone is not duplicate-registration protection; early acknowledgment can lose unfinished work and late acknowledgment allows retries, with additional worker-loss semantics to configure.

rows.name: Celery 4.2.1 with early acknowledgment and an application-level identity ledger
rows.application_scope: Whole composed configuration for a Python task system; Celery provides the worker framework while custom durable state provides logical-task deduplication.
rows.reason: A documented early-acknowledgment mode offers a practical Python worker framework, provided admission deduplication and per-task invocation gating are supplied explicitly.
rows.caveat: Early acknowledgment can lose unfinished work after failure. Do not silently enable task retries or late acknowledgment and still claim a literal no-repeat execution guarantee. Broker behavior, publish uncertainty, long-task limits and worker gating remain unverified.

rows.name: Amazon SQS FIFO queues
rows.application_scope: Managed queue with multiple message groups and renewable visibility for long-running work.
rows.reason: FIFO message deduplication IDs and visibility leases provide managed admission deduplication and distributed claims for independent workers.
rows.caveat: Producer deduplication lasts only a bounded window; visibility expiry or a crash before deletion permits repeat processing, so preserve a durable result ledger.
